newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel keeps shekel down by buying dollars.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel keeps shekel down by buying dollars.

text.p: The shekel's representative rate was fixed lower against the dollar and the basket of foreign currencies on Monday after the Bank of Israel intervened on a relatively high scale by buying dollars, dealers said.
The session opened with heavy conversions of foreign currency on rumours Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would announce a widening of the shekel's trading bands.
Netanyahu is due to speak this evening at an economic conference in the seaside town of Caesarea.
"There are rumours Netanyahu will announce a widening of the bands and further liberalisation of the foreign currency markets," a dealer at United Mizrahi Bank said.

The shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, is allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency at about six percent a year.

"Volume was very high today and we saw heavy conversions despite the fact that the Bank of Israel is expected to lower its key lending rate following the lower-than-expected May CPI," said Zahi Elias of Bank Leumi.
May's consumer price index, released on Sunday, rose 0.5 percent -- well under analysts' expectations of 0.7 to 0.9 percent.
The Bank of Israel is scheduled to announce July interest rates on June 23. The base rate has been unchanged at 13.9 percent since the end of February.
High interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the central bank to intervene heavily in recent months to prevent the currency from appreciating beyond its trading band.
"The central bank was forced again to intervene in the market on a relatively high scale buying almost $150 million," Elias added.

The representative rate for the dollar was fixed at 3.4160 shekels, against 3.4130 on Friday. The basket, composed of the dollar, mark, pound sterling, French franc and yen, was fixed at 3.7066 against 3.7048 on Friday.
On the crosses, the shekel traded against the yen at 2.9953 shekels per 100 yen compared with 2.9867 on Friday, and against the mark at 1.9715 shekels compared with 1.9748 on Friday.
Finance Minister Dan Meridor opposes a widening of the band, while the central bank supports such a move.

Speaking to reporters at Caesarea on Monday, Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said in response to a question on whether a decision has been taken on widening the band: "That's not an issue we need to decide. We are now talking about a variety of measures, all of which are consistent with increasing the freedom of Israelis and investors to operate in the economy, particularly in the area of foreign currency liberalisation.
"In this regard, I believe that the prime minister, the finance minister and myself are getting close to decision".
He would not comment on the timetable.
In late afternoon, the dollar was trading at 3.4130 shekels.
- Dan Gerstenfeld, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
